content: The levels and combinations of nutrients, as well as their interactions, must be carefully considered. This includes evaluating the stability of micronutrient compounds, their physical properties, and their acceptability to consumers. The stability of various micronutrients and their compounds under different cooking processes, which are specific to the context, must be assessed. The relative bioavailability of different chemical forms of micronutrients used in rice fortification, including interactions between nutrients, should be evaluated. The acceptability of any changes in organoleptic characteristics (such as taste, texture, and appearance) resulting from different micronutrient combinations in fortified rice preparations and cooking methods must be determined. The most appropriate delivery platforms for reaching the intended target population should be identified. The effectiveness of different methods for fortifying rice in various contexts must be evaluated. Validated assays for measuring the vitamin and mineral content in fortified rice are essential. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed these evidence-informed recommendations using the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The process included several steps: identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving evidence, assessing and synthesizing the evidence, formulating recommendations (including research priorities), planning for dissemination, addressing equity, human rights, implementation, regulatory and ethical considerations, and evaluating the impact and updating the guideline. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology was employed to prepare evidence profiles related to preselected topics, based on up-to-date systematic reviews and other narrative syntheses of the evidence. The guideline development groups consisted of content experts, methodologists, and representatives of potential stakeholders and beneficiaries. For the development of this guideline, one group participated in a meeting held in Geneva, Switzerland, from February 22–25, 2010, to scope the guideline. A second group participated in a meeting held in Cancun, Mexico, from November 3–6, 2014, to discuss the evidence and finalize the recommendations. Additionally, WHO convened a non-normative dialogue with stakeholders on October 9–10, 2012, in Geneva, Switzerland, to discuss technical considerations for rice fortification in public health. The objective of this dialogue was to review industrial and regulatory technical considerations for rice fortification, as well as considerations for implementing it as a public health strategy, ensuring equitable access and universal coverage. External experts, serving as resource persons, assisted the guideline development group during the process by presenting evidence and identifying research priorities. Four technical experts were invited to peer-review the draft guideline. The WHO steering group will continue to monitor research developments in the area of rice fortification, particularly in areas where evidence is limited or of low certainty. If the guideline requires an update or if concerns arise regarding its validity, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, in collaboration with other WHO departments or programs, will coordinate the update following the formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, along with its internal partners, will conduct a search for appropriate new evidence.
